name: Sensory- and self-motion integration for location
description:
We have developed a novel model in which grid cells combine path integration and environmentally anchored sensory information to generate an optimal estimation of the animal’s current location within an environment. In this framework, the firing of the grid cell population represents a distribution of position probability across space. Path integration is performed by translating this distribution in proportion to the movement of the animal, with associated noise. Sensory information is provided by place cell inputs, whose weights are learned upon exposure to a novel environment. The localisation and learning features together constitute a neurally plausible system capable of performing simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM) [Durrant-Whyte and Bailey 2006]. Weight stabilisation allows the model to account for place cell stabilisation in pre-weanling pups ([Chen et al., in prep], laboratory of Francesca Cacucci, SP3 collaborator). Nonuniform place cell densities can re-create grid cell firing pattern distortions ([3]; figure not shown), and grid patterns rescale in response to environmental manipulations (Figure 1H; [Chen et al., in prep]). Finally reciprocal connections between place and grid cells can produce a change of grid scale in response to changes in path integration gain, with subsequent but diminished effects on the location of associated place cells (Chen et al. (2018), submitted; SP3 collaborator). Simulations have been implemented in Matlab.



Chen G, Lu Y, King JA, Cacucci F, Burgess N. Differential influences of environment and self-motion on place and grid cell firing. Nature communications. 2019 Feb 7;10(1):630.

Chen G, King JA, Lu Y, Cacucci F, Burgess N. Spatial cell firing during virtual navigation of open arenas by head-restrained mice. Elife. 2018 Jun 18;7:e34789.

Durrant-Whyte, Hugh, and Tim Bailey. "Simultaneous localization and mapping: part I." IEEE robotics & automation magazine 13.2 (2006): 99-110.

name: A model of early altered excitability in ventral CA1 pyramidal neurons of TG2576 AD mice
alias: A model of early altered excitability in ventral CA1 pyramidal neurons of TG2576 AD mice
description:
The Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a form of neurodegenerative dementia which causes a progressive decline in cognitive functions. For over 25 years, AD research has been based on the so-called amyloid hypothesis as the main cause of the disease. Its involvement on brain circuit alterations and cellular derailments in very early stages is still under intense investigation. Many studies have been focused on the importance of dopamine and its role within the hippocampal circuitry during AD progression, especially as an early hallmark of the disease. We implemented a computational model that is able to support experimental findings, and suggest experimentally testable predictions, on the cellular mechanisms underlying the early changes in firing properties and the impaired excitability experimentally observed in ventral CA1 pyramidal neurons of Tg2576 mice. The model suggests that the early appearance of cells entering into a depolarization-block state, can be related to an alteration of sodium and potassium currents. In particular, we found that both a shift of sodium channel activation kinetics and the alteration of specific potassium conductances (KDR and KCa) can underlie the altered firing behavior. These results suggest that the early perturbation in the expression or functional involvement of these channels can play a significant role in modulating AP firing behavior of Tg2576 ventral CA1 pyramidal neurons.

For a more detailed description of the model see: 

Spoleti, E., Krashia, P., La Barbera, L., Nobili, A., Lupascu, C. A., Giacalone, E., Keller, F., Migliore, M., Renzi, M., & D'Amelio, M. (2022). Early derailment of firing properties in CA1 pyramidal cells of the ventral hippocampus in an Alzheimer's disease mouse model. *Experimental neurology*, **350**, 113969. [doi:10.1016/j.expneurol.2021.113969](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.expneurol.2021.113969)

name: Sequence learning in a single trial: a spiking neurons model based on hippocampal circuitry
description: In contrast with our everyday experience using brain circuits, it can take a prohibitively long time to train a computational system to produce the correct sequence of outputs in the presence of a series of inputs. This suggests that something important is missing in the way in which models are trying to reproduce basic cognitive functions. In this work, we introduce a new neuronal network architecture that is able to learn, in a single trial, an arbitrary long sequence of any known objects. The key point of the model is the explicit use of mechanisms and circuitry observed in the hippocampus, which allow the model to reach a level of efficiency and accuracy that, to the best of our knowledge, is not possible with abstract network implementations. By directly following the natural system’s layout and circuitry, this type of implementation has the additional advantage that the results can be more easily compared to the experimental data, allowing a deeper and more direct understanding of the mechanisms underlying cognitive functions and dysfunctions and opening the way to a new generation of learning architectures.

name: CA1 Human hippocampus network for single point neuron simulations
description:
This is a full-scale scaffold model of the human hippocampus CA1 area, based on data obtained from the analysis of histological human brain images, which are publicly available from the BigBrain Jülich repository. A custom-made computational algorithm has been developed to extract from the images the positions of neuronal somata.

A second custom made algorithm has been developed to connect neurons following morpho-anatomical landmarks. The full matrix of neuronal positioning together with the indices of connected neurons is provided as a connection matrix in order to be used for large-scale simulation with single point neurons.


The data are organized as follows:

1. The Neuronal placement text file `HUMAN_PLACEMENT_4_8M_Pyr.txt` allows generating the complete human CA1 scaffold. It contains 4 columns containing the 3D coordinates and the GID (Global Index) of pyramidal cells and interneurons of the human CA1 hippocampus obtained from the image analysis of the histological sections of a full brain downloaded from the BigBrain repository.
2. The connectivity matrices in the hdf5 files allow to generate the full matrix of connection pairs. Each dataset in the hdf5 files contains a set of 2-column arrays with the pairs of numbers indicating the GID of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons connected with the developed algorithm.
3. The two directories `long_simdata_human_01ffa4a7-a809-43f5-83c1-5cc839a1dc52_only_exc_connections/` and `long_simdata_human_5f859adf-469c-4f37-89e6-9d2e13f776da_inh_movie_paper/` contain data generated by running simulations with either only the excitatory connections or both the excitatory and inhibitory connections, to allow the inspection of simulation results without having to run the simulations.

## Instructions to run the model.

The scripts to run the simulation are in the `hippocampus_human_collab` directory. Running the model currently requires an account on Piz Daint at [CSCS](https://https://www.cscs.ch).
The model is made to run on NEST. NEST is available in a Docker image that has to be loaded using Sarus on Piz Daint. The script `sarus_load_image.sh` takes care of loading the Docker image `showcase_2.tar` on Sarus. The authors thank Lionel Kusch (Aix Marseille University) for the technical assistance in compiling the NEST simulator in a Docker image.

To run the model:

- Download the following files and directories:
    * `hippocampus_human_collab/placement_connections_scaffold.hdf5` (80 GB!!!)
    * `inh_remapped/` (39 GB).
- Copy the files `helper.py`, `synaptic_models.py`, `neuron_models.py` from  `"long_simdata_human_01ffa4a7-a809-43f5-83c1-5cc839a1dc52_only_exc_connections/"` to `"hippocampus_human_collab/"`.
- Set the correct path `"input_hdf5_data_dir"` in the beginning of the `run_nest_serialized_connect.py` script to point to the location of the 
`placement_connections_scaffold.hdf5`
- Set the correct account for HPC resources in `run_sarus_normal.sh`.
- Run by executing the bash script: `Start_Human_Hippocampus.sh`

The script will create a directory in your $SCRATCH dir and store the simulation data.

Before running consider that a single simulation takes up to 3 hours to complete and uses 2400 CPU hours from your HPC account.

For support contact Sergio Solinas.

name: Scaffold model of mouse CA1 hippocampus
description:
The linked Jupyter notebook allows to generate a network of CA1 pyramidal cells with probability cloud morphologies. 

The script implements an algorithm based on morpho-anatomical landmarks allowing to construct geometrical axons and dendrites mimicked by ellipsoids and cones respectively. Neurites are oriented according to their relative position within the CA1 volume and in relation to the minimum distance from the CA3 and Subiculum regions. The connections of each neuron are calculated by intersecting axons of every pyramidal cell and the dendrites of all the remaining cells. This procedure allows to generate the connectivity matrix required to build a point neuron network of CA1 pyramidal cells. The full network or alternatively other brain areas can be replicated by adopting the same morpho-anatomical strategy.

name: Dendritic processing in hippocampal pyramidal cells - Kali & Freund, 2004
description:
Area CA1 of the hippocampus contains a population of pyramidal cells, accompanied by a diverse array of inhibitory interneurons, which are believed to modulate the activity and plasticity of pyramidal neurons. 
This model creates detailed models of hippocampal principal cells and interneurons, which can be used to explore how these different cell types interact within the hippocampal network.

A model of CA1 pyramidal neurons, as described in:

name: CA1 hypofunction in schizophrenia
description:
A model of CA1 pyramidal neurons, as described in:

M. Migliore, I. De Blasi, D. Tegolo, R. Migliore (2011) A modeling study suggesting how a reduction in the context-dependent input on CA1 pyramidal neurons could generate schizophrenic behavior. *Neural Networks* **24**:552-559 [doi:10.1016/j.neunet.2011.01.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2011.01.001)

The model (ModelDB accession number: 138205) was used to study schizophrenic behaviour, and is based on models from the same modeling group, which were used to investigate the initiation and propagation of action potentials in oblique dendrites, and have been validated against a number of different electrophysiological data.

name: Dichotomy of action-potential backpropagation in CA1 pyramidal neuron dendrites (Golding et al 2001)
description:
A model of CA1 pyramidal neurons (ModelDB accession number: 64167), as described in:

Golding NL, Kath WL, Spruston N (2001) Dichotomy of action-potential backpropagation in CA1 pyramidal neuron dendrites. *J. Neurophysiol.* **86**:2998-3010 [doi:10.1152/jn.2001.86.6.2998](http://doi.org/10.1152/jn.2001.86.6.2998)

The model was developed to show the dichotomy of the back-propagation efficacy and the amplitudes of the back-propagating action potentials at distal trunk regions in CA1 pyramidal cells and to make predictions on the possible causes of this behaviour. It contains only the most important ion channels (Na, KDR,KA) needed to reproduce the generation and propagation of action potentials. Here we tested three different versions of the model: the ones belonging to the Figure 8 A, Figure 8 B and Figure 9 B of the corresponding paper.

name: Linear vs non-linear integration in CA1 oblique dendrites (Gómez González et al. 2011)
description:
A model of CA1 pyramidal neurons (ModelDB accession number: 144450), described in:

Gómez González JF, Mel BW, Poirazi P (2011) Distinguishing Linear vs. Non-Linear Integration in CA1 Radial Oblique Dendrites: It's about Time. *Front. Comput. Neurosci.* **5**:44. [doi:10.3389/fncom.2011.00044](http://doi.org/10.3389/fncom.2011.00044) 

The model is based on the [Poirazi et al. (2003) model](https://model-catalog.brainsimulation.eu/#model_id.4c5d8992-f2d4-43ad-bb27-23b98836e59b), which was modified to replicate the experimental data of [Losonczy and Magee (2006)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2006.03.016) on the nonlinear signal integration of radial oblique dendrites when the inputs arrive in a short time window. The model was adjusted to five different detailed morphologies.

We provide here:
- a link to the original model code on ModelDB, including all five morphologies
- Python wrappers for the SciUnit model validation framework. Each morphology is provided as a separate version of the model.

description: The Poirazi et al. name: A two-stage model of dendritic integration in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Katz et al., 2009)
description:
A model of hippocampus CA1 pyramidal neurons (ModelDB accession number: 127351), described in:

Katz Y, Menon V, Nicholson DA, Geinisman Y, Kath WL, Spruston N (2009) Synapse distribution suggests a two-stage model of dendritic integration in CA1 pyramidal neurons. *Neuron* **63**:171-7 [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2009.06.023](http://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2009.06.023)

and based on the Golding et al. (2001) model. It was built to investigate the functional consequences of the distribution of strength and density of synapses on the apical dendrites, as observed experimentally, on the mode of dendritic integration.

We provide here both the original code (via ModelDB) and a version with a Python wrapper for the SciUnit model validation framework.

name: Model-based spatial navigation in the hippocampus - ventral striatum circuit
description:
The computational model explores the links between model-based reinforcement learning (MB-RL) and the functioning of the hippocampus (HC) and the ventral striatum (vStr):  a neuronal circuit that is increasingly recognized as an appropriate model system to understand goal-directed (spatial) decisions and planning mechanisms in the brain. 

We tested the MB-RL agent in a contextual conditioning task that depends on intact hippocampus and ventral striatal (shell) function and show that it solves the task while showing key behavioral and neuronal signatures of the HC—vStr circuit. Our simulations also explore the benefits of biological forms of look-ahead prediction (forward sweeps) during both learning and control. This model thus contributes to fill the gap between our current understanding of computational algorithms and biological realizations of (model-based) reinforcement learning.

The model is fully described in "Stoianov IP, Pennartz CMA, Lansink CS, Pezzulo G (2018) Model-based spatial navigation in the hippocampus-ventral striatum circuit: A computational analysis. PLoS Comput Biol 14(9): e1006316. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006316"

Note that the model has been also implemented in the Neurorobotics platform:
https://collab.humanbrainproject.eu/#/collab/78682/nav/532632

name: Hippocampal formation as a hierarchical generative model
description:
This is a computational model that casts the hippocampal formation as a hierarchical generative model that organizes sequential experiences, such as such as rodent trajectories during spatial navigation, into coherent spatiotemporal contexts. The model addresses the formation of spatial maps (in the hippocampus) and the the offline resampling of fictive sequences from the generative model (aka generative replay) for the sake of continual learning of multiple sequential experiences. It reproduces several empirical findings on internally generated hippocampal sequences (e.g., replays). It can also be used to analyze the spatial codes that emerge in the hippocampus during spatial learning; and replay dynamics. 

The computational model is described in the preprint publication P2331: Stoianov I., Maisto D., Pezzulo G., (2020) The hippocampal formation as a hierarchical generative model supporting generative replay and continual learning. BiorXiv preprint (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.01.16.908889v1.full)

name: The hippocampus-ventral striatum circuit model in the Neurorobotics Platform
description:
### Introduction

The hippocampus is a complex structure of the brain which is part of the limbic system, and it is mainly involved in the development of long-term memory and spatial memory. In fact, the hippocampus makes use of the grid cells present in the entorhinal cortex to generate place cells, specific types of neurons that fire when the animal enters a particular place in the environment. What allows an animal to learn how to navigate in this environment is the basal ganglia (BG) circuit, composed of many subnuclei located in different areas of the brain: this circuit, thanks to a neurotransmitter called dopamine, changes the synaptic strengths of the striatum, a subnucleus of the BG, and makes the animal be able to select actions in its environment in order to maximize some reward, a mechanism very similar to reinforcement learning.

Stoianov et al. proposed a probabilistic model which simulates the functioning of these neural circuits, and tested it on three different tasks on a Y-maze environment: in the first task (cue conditioning), every final position had a 100% probability to give a reward, while on the second task (context conditioning) the reward probabilities varied depending on the room; finally, a third task was performed (contextual conditioning) with reward probabilities of 0% in order to check the spatial preferences learned by the robot during the previous phases of training. The rodent was able to find out the reward locations that yielded a higher probability to get the reward. However, the model was tested on a simple environment without a realistic agent and sensors, though a noise term was added for the retrieval of the position and direction of the rodent, and for the execution of the actions.

In order to find out how this model would perform in a realistic scenario, we integrated it on the NRP and performed simulations on more complex environments. The NRP is a simulation infrastructure that aims to bridge the gap between neuroscience and robotics by providing biologically realistic brain models to virtually embodied agents, and vice versa. For these simulations, we employed the Husky robot, an unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) with four wheels and realistic sensors.

### NRP Integration

In order to integrate the Matlab model in the Neurorobotics Platform (NRP), we utilized the Matlab engine, a Python package that allows executing Matlab function from Python scripts. The simulation environment, including initialization of the world, execution of actions and visiting reward locations, is handled by the NRP, while the Matlab functions for control and learning are called from Python through the Matlab engine.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, we tested the model on three different mazes: a simple grid with 8 reward locations, a T-maze with 6 reward locations, and a 4 rooms environment with 12 reward locations. The Husky robot uses a physically realistic laser scan to check if there are obstacles nearby, in order to stop when it is approaching a wall.

![Figure 1](https://object.cscs.ch/v1/AUTH_64bf8536ad8b4872a4121f909be7e82f/Falotico/hippocampus-ventral-striatum/figures/fig1_900px.png)

### Results

Fig. 2 shows the metric scores for the simple environment, Fig. 3 represents the scores for the T-maze, while Fig. 4 shows the scores for the 4 rooms environment. Both simulations consisted of 1000 trials.

In order to assess the model performances in a robotic scenario, we relied on the four metrics used on the original work: (i) accuracy (number of trials where the rodent finds a reward location over the number of trials); (ii) path length of each trial (a lower path length means that the rodent found the reward location in few steps); (iii) sweep depth for each trial; (iv) decision certainty of the rodent.

As can be seen from the scores, the Husky robot is able to learn the first two tasks, while the decision certainty decreases; on the other hand, it has more difficulties learning the third task, due to the increased complexity of the environment.

![Figure 2](https://object.cscs.ch/v1/AUTH_64bf8536ad8b4872a4121f909be7e82f/Falotico/hippocampus-ventral-striatum/figures/fig2_600px.png)
![Figure 3](https://object.cscs.ch/v1/AUTH_64bf8536ad8b4872a4121f909be7e82f/Falotico/hippocampus-ventral-striatum/figures/fig3_600px.png)
![Figure 4](https://object.cscs.ch/v1/AUTH_64bf8536ad8b4872a4121f909be7e82f/Falotico/hippocampus-ventral-striatum/figures/fig4_600px.png)

name: Hippocampal & Striatal navigation
description:
Behavioural and neural data suggest that multiple strategies and brain systems support learning about reward. Reinforcement learning (RL) considers these strategies in terms of model-based (MB) learning, which involves learning an explicit transition model of the available state-space, or model-free (MF) learning, which involves directly estimating the cumulative future reward associated with each state. The MB-MF distinction parallels that between place learning and response learning within spatial navigation. Lesion and inactivation studies suggests that dorsal hippocampus (dHC) underlies both MB and place learning, whereas dorsolateral striatum (DLS) underlies MF and response learning. Here, we present a computational model of the dHC and DLS contributions to reward learning that applies to spatial and nonspatial domains. In the model, hippocampal place cell firing reflects the geodesic distance of other states from its preferred state along the graph of task structure. Accordingly, this population can support a value function or goal cell firing rate, via one-shot learning, on which gradient ascent corresponds to taking the shortest path on the graph, behaviour associated with MB planning. In contrast, the DLS learns through MF stimulus-response associations with egocentric environmental cues. We show that this model reproduces animal behaviour on spatial navigation tasks using the Morris Water Maze and the Plus Maze, and human behaviour on non-spatial two-step decision tasks. We discuss how the geodesic place cell fields could be learnt, and how this type of representation helps to span the gap between MB and MF learning. The generality of our model, originally shaped by detailed constraints in the spatial literature, suggests that the hippocampal-striatal system is a general-purpose learning device that adaptively combines MB and MF mechanisms.  

[Detailed description of simulations and results](https://github.com/bicanski/HBPcollab/blob/master/Striatal_v_hippocampal_nav_v2/Modelling_hippocampal_and_dorsolateral_striatal_contributions_to_learning_across_domains.pdf)

name: Age-dependent excitability of CA1 pyramidal neurons in APPPS1 Alzheimer's model
description: Age-dependent accumulation of amyloid-b, provoking increasing brain amyloidopathy, triggers abnormal patterns of neuron activity and circuit synchronization in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) as observed in human AD patients and AD mouse models. Recent studies on AD mouse models, mimicking this age-dependent amyloidopathy, identified alterations in CA1 neuron excitability. However, these models generally also overexpress mutated amyloid precursor protein (APP) and presenilin 1 (PS1) and there is a lack of a clear correlation of neuronal excitability alterations with progressive amyloidopathy. The active development of computational models of AD points out the need of collecting such experimental data to build a reliable disease model exhibiting AD-like disease progression. We therefore used the feature extraction tool of the Human Brain Project (HBP) Brain Simulation Platform to systematically analyze the excitability profile of CA1 pyramidal neuron in the APPPS1 mouse model. We identified specific features of neuron excitability that best correlate either with over-expression of mutated APP and PS1 or increasing Ab amyloidopathy. Notably, we report strong alterations in membrane time constant and action potential width and weak alterations in firing behavior. Also, using a CA1 pyramidal neuron model, we evidence amyloidopathy-dependent alterations in Ih. Finally, cluster analysis of these recordings showed that we could reliably assign a trace to its correct group, opening the door to a more refined, less variable analysis of AD-affected neurons. This inter-disciplinary analysis, bringing together experimentalists and modelers, helps to further unravel the neuronal mechanisms most affected by AD and to build a biologically plausible computational model of the AD brain.

name: Theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling in a hippocampal CA1 microcircuit
description:
## Model Description

This project implements a hippocampal microcircuit model demonstrating
how **theta–gamma phase–amplitude coupling (PAC)** can naturally emerge
from a simple feedback mechanism. The circuit consists of interacting
excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations whose dynamics give rise
to **theta-frequency oscillations modulating higher-frequency gamma
bursts**.

---

## Instructions to Run the Model

All simulation scripts are located in the main project directory.

The model is implemented using **NetPyNE** on top of the **NEURON
simulator** and is intended to run on a **High-Performance Computing
(HPC)** system. Due to the network size and computational demands, it is
not suitable for execution on a standard local workstation.

---

## Requirements

- Python ≥ 3.8
- NEURON (compiled with MPI support)
- NetPyNE
- MPI implementation (e.g., OpenMPI or Intel MPI)

---

## HPC Environment Setup

Load the required modules:

module load python/3.11.7--gcc--10.2.0
module load openmpi
module load mpi

Activate your Python environment and install dependencies:

pip install NEURON==8.2.6
pip install netpyne==1.0.7

Verify that NEURON is compiled with MPI support:

nrniv -mpi

---

## Compile Mechanisms

nrnivmodl mechanisms

---

## Run a Single Simulation (MPI)

 From the main project directory:

mpiexec -n <NUM_PROCESSES> nrniv -mpi init.py

Replace <NUM_PROCESSES> with the number of MPI processes allocated by
your HPC scheduler.

---

## Batch Simulations

After verifying that a single simulation runs correctly, configure your
HPC account settings in `t42_batch.py`.

Then execute:

nrniv -python t42_batch.py

---

## Outputs

Simulation outputs are saved in directories such as `t42data*`.

Each run generates:

- t42XYcfg.json — simulation configuration
- t42XYdata.json — simulation results

name: A model of presynaptic Kv7 channel function in hippocampal mossy fiber boutons - Martinello et al. 2019
alias: A model of presynaptic Kv7 channel function in hippocampal mossy fiber boutons - Martinello et al. 2019
description:
In hippocampus, a type of slowly-activated and non-inactivating K+ channels, belonging to the Kv7 family, are highly localized on initial segments of myelinated and unmyelinated axons where they influence neuronal excitability. Interestingly, immunohistochemistry shows that the KV7.2 and KV7.3 subunits are localized throughout hippocampal mossy fibers. Electrophysiological recordings from mature synaptic boutons showed that the KV7/M- current is also present here, is active at rest and enhances the membrane conductance. The current also reduces the spike half-width and afterdepolatization (ADP) following a presynaptic spike. This is likely to have significant consequences for the modulation of excitatory neurotransmitter release from these boutons, and thus signal transmission, at DG-CA3 synapses. We implemented a biophysical computational model of a mossy fiber bouton (MFB) in order to highlight the mechanisms underlying the ADP observed after Kv7 channels block. The model is able to reproduce a number of experimental findings under control and after Kv7 current block by XE991. The results suggest that Kv7 conductance limits spike-induced rise in Ca2+ concentration and regulates spike width and ADP amplitude. The model suggests that the ADP is caused by a relatively slow Ca2+-dependent mechanism, which can be conveniently modelled as a slow deactivation time constant of the Ca2+ current in MFB. This is a new feature that has not been previously observed experimentally. Taken together, these results suggest that presynaptic Kv7 channels expression at the mossy fiber-CA3 synapse may have an important role in modulating synaptic transmission and signal coding in the hippocampus network.

For a more detailed description of the model see:

Martinello, K., Giacalone, E., Migliore, M., Brown, D. A., & Shah, M. M. (2019). The subthreshold-active KV7 current regulates neurotransmission by limiting spike-induced Ca2+ influx in hippocampal mossy fiber synaptic terminals. *Communications biology*, **2**, 145. [doi:10.1038/s42003-019-0408-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0408-4)

For more implementation details, see Evans and Burgess (2019), NeurIPS.
